lessons.title: तीस चालीस (tīs cālīs) — two rungs past where the counting stopped
lessons.gloss: thirty and forty — the first two rungs past the twenty the counting stopped at

segments.text: Count from ग्यारह to बीस. Then stop, because that is where your counting has ended until now.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: तीस, चालीस

segments.text: तीस (tīs) — thirty.
चालीस (cālīs) — forty.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the tens are the part worth learning

segments.text: Say those three in a row and the family resemblance is audible: –ीस at the end of all of them. It is the same ending, worn down from the same Sanskrit word for ten, and it will carry you as far as fifty.

तीन is three and तीस is thirty. चार is four and चालीस is forty. The openings are not identical to the small numbers, but they are close enough to hold on to, and that is the most help Hindi gives with numbers at this size.

lessons.title: पचास साठ (pacās sāṭh) — where the pattern stops helping
lessons.gloss: fifty and sixty — the last of the shared ending, and the first word that goes its own way

segments.text: Say बीस, तीस, चालीस. Listen to the ending they share.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: पचास, साठ

segments.text: पचास (pacās) — fifty.
साठ (sāṭh) — sixty.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one keeps the ending, one drops it

utterances: number: 40. word: चालीस. the shared ending: yes.
number: 50. word: पचास. the shared ending: a worn version.
number: 60. word: साठ. the shared ending: gone.

segments.text: पचास still leans on पाँच, the five you have counted since the opening chapters, and it still carries a trace of that ending. साठ leans on छह and keeps nothing else.
That is the shape of the rest of this chapter: the words get less helpful as the numbers get bigger. Knowing that in advance is worth more than a rule that would not hold.
पचास is the one to hold on to hardest. It is the price on a tea stall sign and the age of somebody's father, and it is the most common of the four so far.

lessons.title: सत्तर अस्सी नब्बे (sattar assī nabbe) — the last three rungs
lessons.gloss: seventy, eighty and ninety — three words that lean on the small numbers and keep almost nothing else

segments.text: Say पचास and साठ. One of them kept the old ending and one dropped it.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: सत्तर, अस्सी, नब्बे

segments.text: सत्तर (sattar) — seventy.
अस्सी (assī) — eighty.
नब्बे (nabbe) — ninety.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: each one leans on a number you already count

utterances: small number: सात. ten times it: सत्तर.
small number: आठ. ten times it: अस्सी.
small number: नौ. ten times it: नब्बे.

segments.text: Read that table down the left and you are counting seven, eight, nine — which you have done since early on. Read it down the right and you are counting seventy, eighty, ninety.
The opening consonant survives in all three, and that is the whole of the help on offer. Beyond the first sound, each word has been worn into its own shape and has to be met as a word.
Say the pairs across, one after another: sāt, sattar. āṭh, assī. nau, nabbe. Hearing them together is what makes them stick.

lessons.title: गिनती की तालिका (gintī kī tālikā) — eight rungs, and what sits between them
lessons.gloss: the counting table — the eight rungs together, and an honest account of what sits between them

segments.text: Say the last of the three words you met, the one for ninety.
Eight words, on top of the hundred you already say. Every price, every age and every house number you are likely to meet sits on or between them.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: what sits between them

segments.text: Here is the honest part, and it is better to hear it than to guess wrong.
Hindi puts the small number first. Twenty-five is five-twenty: पच्चीस (paccīs) opens with the sound of पाँच. Twenty-two is बाईस (bāīs) and opens with दो's vowel.
That order is the opposite of English, and it is the one thing about the in-between numbers a learner can rely on.

What a learner cannot rely on is reassembling them. पच्चीस is not पाँच and बीस stuck together in any way you could work out from the pieces — the two halves have worn into each other. Each of the numbers between the rungs is its own word, and they are met one at a time, over a long while.
So: recognise the shape, know the small number is in front, and learn the rungs cold. That is the part that pays.

lessons.title: पचास रुपये (pacās rupaye) — a price, said out loud
lessons.gloss: fifty rupees — a price said out loud, which is a number and a word you already had

segments.text: Say the word for a rupee. You learned where its name came from — a piece of metal that has been given a shape.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: put the two together

segments.text: पचास रुपये (pacās rupaye) — fifty rupees.
Number first, then the thing. That is the whole construction, and you have both halves already: the number arrived in this chapter and the rupee arrived a long way back.
रुपये rather than रुपया, because more than one is being counted. That bend is the same one the track has been making since the adjectives, and it costs nothing new here.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the prices you can now read

utterances: पचास रुपये (pacās rupaye) means fifty rupees.
सौ रुपये means a hundred rupees.

segments.text: Five prices, and between them most of what a tea stall, a bus fare or a bag of vegetables will ask of you.

This is what the counting was for. A number on its own is a recitation; a number in front of a thing is a price, an age or an address, and that is where the nine rungs stop being a list and start being useful.
